en: *The Sutra on Prince Huixiu*, one fascicle.
Sengyou’s Catalogue states that the translator is lost; it is now appended to the Western Jin records.
The Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, together with ten thousand bodhisattvas.
There were one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, along with numerous upāsakas and upāsikās, as well as innumerable deva kings, Brahmā, Śakra, humans, spirits, and nāgas, all seated together.

The Crown Prince of King Ajātaśatru, named Udayibhadra, accompanied by five hundred sons of elders, each holding a golden-flower parasol, set out from the city of Rājagṛha. Following the Crown Prince, they all arrived at the place where the Buddha was. Having each offered their parasols to the Buddha, they joined their palms, prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground to pay homage to the Buddha, and then withdrew to stand before him.
The Prince joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does a Bodhisattva attain such physical beauty?
By what causes and conditions is he not born from within a woman’s womb, but instead born within a lotus flower?"
“By what causes and conditions does one know the past lives of former existences?
I pray that the Buddha will bestow great grace upon me and explain this to me in detail.
The Buddha told the Prince:
“Bodhisattvas who practice patience and harbor no anger will, in future lives, be born as humans with handsome and upright features.

Bodhisattvas who refrain from lust and do not engage in sexual intercourse with women will, in future lives, not enter the wombs of women, but rather be born through transformation within lotus flowers.”

"A Bodhisattva delights in upholding the sutras and precepts and teaching others; consequently, in future lives, he will spontaneously know the events of his own past existences throughout incalculable eons.
The Prince said to the Buddha, "By what causes and conditions does a Bodhisattva possess the thirty-two marks?"
"By what causes and conditions are there eighty secondary marks?
By what causes and conditions do people never tire of beholding the physical form of the Buddha?
The Buddha told the Prince:
"When I was originally a bodhisattva, I delighted in practicing generosity for others.

Whatever they sought—whether clothing, food and drink, gold, silver, rare treasures, carriages and horses, male and female slaves, wives and children, or even flesh, limbs, head, and eyes—I never opposed their requests. Without any greed or stinginess, I gave them all; by virtue of this, I attained the thirty-two marks."

The Bodhisattva, with a heart of loving-kindness, takes pity on the people and all classes of wriggling and crawling creatures, regarding them as if they were his own infant children; desiring to deliver and liberate them, he thereby attains the eighty secondary marks.

The Bodhisattva regards an enemy as he does his own parents; his mind is perfectly equanimous and without distinction. For this reason, when people behold the physical form of the Buddha, they never tire of gazing upon it.
The Prince addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva come to know the wisdom of the profound sūtras?
By what causes and conditions does he come to know the peace and stability of samādhi?”
"For what reason do all the words spoken by the Buddha cause those who hear them to rejoice?
The Buddha told the Prince:
"The Bodhisattva delights in copying the sutras, reciting them, studying them, and explaining them; for this reason, he understands the wisdom of the profound sutras."
The Bodhisattva always delights in concentration and mental tranquility; for this reason, he attains the peace and stability of samādhi.
All that the Bodhisattva speaks is sincere and does not deceive or weary others; for this reason, his words are truthful and trustworthy, and all who hear them rejoice.
The Prince addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what causes and conditions are the actions of a bodhisattva’s body, the words of his mouth, and the thoughts of his mind all pure?
By what causes and conditions is Māra unable to find an opportunity against him?”
"For what reason do the multitude not dare to slander the Buddha’s sutras and the Way?
Why do they not dare to slander the community of bhikṣus?
The Buddha told the prince:
“The Bodhisattva delights in attending upon the Buddha, delights in the Way of the Sūtras, and delights in the community of Bhikṣus; for this reason, he attains purity.
The Bodhisattva practices walking meditation with diligence day and night; for this reason, Māra cannot find an opportunity to harm him.”

Whatever the bodhisattva speaks is entirely sincere and without deception; for this reason, the people do not dare to slander the Buddha’s sutras and the Way, nor do they dare to slander the community of bhikṣus.
The Prince addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva attain a long life?
By what causes and conditions does one become free from illness?”
"For what cause and condition do all members of one's household live in harmony and mutual respect, such that others are not caused to be separated?
The Buddha told the Prince:
"The Bodhisattva possesses a mind of loving-kindness and does not kill living beings; for this reason, in future lives, he attains a long lifespan."
A bodhisattva does not carry weapons or staves to terrify others; for this reason, when born in future lives, they will be free from illness.

When a bodhisattva sees people engaged in conflict, they take pleasure in intervening to resolve it and bring about reconciliation; for this reason, when born in future lives, they will not be separated from others.
The Prince addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva easily obtain wealth and possessions, such that being rich is not difficult?
By what causes and conditions does one not lose one's wealth, nor have it plundered or stolen by others?"
"By what causes and conditions does a noble person attain such great wealth?
The Buddha told the prince:
"A bodhisattva possesses wisdom and discernment and is not foolish; for this reason, it is not difficult for him to attain great riches."

The Bodhisattva delights in giving; he does not covet or begrudge what remains, nor does he lose his wealth. Seeing others possess riches and enjoyments or acquire money and property, he feels no envy. For these reasons, he becomes a venerable one.
"A Bodhisattva does not kill and is not conceited; for this reason, he attains the status of one who is noble and wealthy.
The Prince addressed the Buddha, saying, "By what causes and conditions does a Bodhisattva attain the divine eye that sees through all things?"
"By what causes and conditions does the divine ear hear through all things?
By what causes and conditions does one come to know the destinies of birth and death in the world, as well as their goodness and evil?
The Buddha told the prince:
"Bodhisattvas delight in lighting lamps within Buddhist temples; by virtue of this, they attain the divine eye that sees through all things.
Bodhisattvas delight in offering songs, music, and dance within Buddhist temples; by virtue of this, they attain the divine ear that hears everything."
"The Bodhisattva enters samādhi and attains dhyāna; by means of this, he knows the destinies of birth and death in the world, as well as good and evil.
The Prince addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does the Bodhisattva attain the four bases of supernormal power for flying?"
"By what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva attain the recollection of events from incalculable kalpas of past lives?
By what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva attain Buddhahood and then pass away?
The Buddha told the prince:

"When a bodhisattva practices giving, bestowing chariots, horses, elephants, as well as mules, donkeys, camels, and sandals upon others, by means of this, they attain the four bases of supernatural power for flying."

The Bodhisattva delights in mindfulness of the Buddhas, samādhi, and the bases of spiritual power (ṛddhipāda); by training in this and teaching others to delight in it, he thereby attains the ability to recollect events from incalculable kalpas of past lives.
“The Bodhisattva attains the Buddha’s mind and is without attachment; for this reason, he enters parinirvāṇa and brings his life to an end.
The Prince addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what causes and conditions does a Bodhisattva pre-arrange the Buddha-field?”
"For what causes and conditions do you know in advance that you will obtain the community of bhikṣus in future lives?
For what causes and conditions do you obtain light that shines universally throughout the ten directions?
The Buddha told the prince:
“Bodhisattvas constantly have many vows; for this reason, they pre-prepare the Buddha-fields.
Bodhisattvas give alms to the people and delight in teaching others to practice the six *pāramitās*; for this reason, they later obtain a community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*).”

"A Bodhisattva takes objects of the seven treasures and fashions them into parasols, which he offers above the Buddha and his temples; for this reason, he attains a radiance that shines universally throughout the ten directions.
When the Buddha explained these matters in detail for the sake of the Prince, the Prince was filled with great joy, as were the five hundred sons of the elders.
The Crown Prince addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Will I fully receive and practice everything that the Buddhas of future ages shall preach?
The Buddha laughed heartily, and from his mouth issued light of five colors that illuminated the ten directions.
Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause.
By what causes and conditions have these five-colored rays of light been emitted to illuminate the ten directions?"
The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"Listen as I speak of this.
Prince Huixiu and the five hundred sons of elders, in their previous lives, made offerings to ten billion Buddhas and all practiced the path of the bodhisattva."

In the past, during the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, these five hundred people were all disciples taught by me; in a future age, they shall all meet together and make offerings to six hundred million Buddhas.
One kalpa hence, there will be a kalpa named Mahāpāramitā; within that single kalpa, five hundred people, both preceding and following one another, shall all share the same name: Yaśottara Dhūtaguṇa.

When he later becomes a Buddha, his land shall be like the land of Amitābha Buddha; the bodhisattvas therein who travel back and forth by flight and those who manifest transformations shall all be like the bodhisattvas in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

Those who hear this sutra shall all be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha as bodhisattvas, like Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; in future ages, they shall become Buddhas just as Amitābha Buddha has done.

When the sutra had been spoken, Prince Huixiu, along with five hundred sons of elders, the assembly of bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as devas, brahmās, humans, ghosts, spirits, and nāgas, were all greatly rejoiced; they came forward, prostrated before the Buddha, and departed.
The Sūtra on Prince Huixiu Spoken by the Buddha
